title: Global liquidity peaks: the companies that spent most aggressively on AI in H1 are the first to be discounted
dek: A rising capital market requires new money to keep buying in. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that invested most aggressively in AI in the first half are shifting from being rewarded to being discounted.
why: It puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPOs and household balance sheets on the same funding chain, offering a macro framework that does not treat AI as a panacea.
who: For investors watching both US AI stocks and China/Hong Kong asset allocation, and for primary-market practitioners judging the sources and pace of hot money in 2025.
skip: The case-by-case discussion of Hong Kong IPOs can be skipped; the main thread starts at 8:11 with Nvidia's liquidity experiment.

points.h: A low IPO break rate is not a good signal
points.body: Do not take the low first-day break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of a strengthening market. In the first half of this year the break rate was only in the teens, far below the roughly fifty-fifty level normal under a market mechanism, meaning that those participating in IPOs were mainly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently the supply of listed companies has decreased and IPO-related funds have run into problems, yet the two newly listed companies still broke issue, showing that temporary supply-side control has not solved the fundamental problem: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

points.h: The more aggressive the AI spending, the sooner the punishment
points.body: Market attitude reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI CapEx, the higher the valuation. By the time half-year reports were disclosed in late July, any large internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in the first half, especially those that spent all their free cash flow, was discounted—even Google was not exempt. Q2 was precisely the quarter of the most FOMO across the entire supply chain, with everyone afraid of price increases and rushing to spend money first; inventories could still support gross margins. By Q3, inventories are depleted and the impact of price increases returns, so unfavorable factors will appear together.

points.h: Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
points.body: Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco introduced 'lease-to-buy' to help customers finance, recognizing future revenue as sales revenue in advance; Nvidia is now also pushing lease-to-buy. In the financial report, free cash flow halved quarter-on-quarter, and accounts receivable on the books are far above historical levels—this is suspected to be partly related to the credit enhancement and collection structure brought by lease-to-buy. Therefore Nvidia may have reached a stage where it needs more aggressive financial tactics to maintain capital market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

points.h: Primary-market money comes from bullets fired three years ago
points.body: The answer lies in the timing of fund fundraising. The money concentrated in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022; they barely invested in 2023-2025, until they saw state capital betting and earning the most during a period when no one dared to invest—the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large models, and two large chips stimulated market-based funds. Everyone's mentality is: copy the state capital's homework. So this is not a rational long-term incremental wave, but more like a delayed emotional release.

points.h: New real estate policy removes residents from the financing chain
points.body: The key to recent real estate policy is not to bail out developers, but to pull residents out of the old financing cycle. In the past, buying pre-sale housing meant residents took on the role of financing targets in the investment-driven chain: pay first, receive housing later. After the policy pushes the chain toward marketization, buyers get completed housing and only bear the consumer role, with risk reset back to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when housing prices were near the bottom, in order to first stabilize the denominator on the asset side and avoid panic from breaking the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries have followed similar paths.

points.h: A slow bull is not a slogan, it is a chip structure
points.body: A slow bull does not rely on slogans, but on layering market chips by duration: the bottom layer is low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips taken up by insurance, as long money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, playing a quasi-stabilizing role; Central Huijin and China Securities Finance adjust the index at a higher layer; the top layer is retail investors, private funds and active management funds. The new insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in term, return and liquidity, which institutionally ensures long money for long investments, medium money for medium investments, and short money for short investments—not allowing short-term public money to be invested in ten-year low-liquidity assets.

points.h: Crises are rescued bigger and bigger, at least one and a half bubbles
points.body: After the US dollar detached from gold in 1971, global central banks became increasingly accustomed to directly intervening in crises by printing money, acting faster each time. The quantitative easing after 2008 should have been cleared during the rate hike cycle, but was interrupted by political intervention, and then the pandemic hit in 2020, so a larger wave of easing was layered on top before the previous bubble had dissipated—today at least one and a half bubbles have accumulated. Central bank governors have learned to print more money immediately when a crisis first appears, and the endogenous result is that inflation, rising financial assets and wealth polarization intensify simultaneously. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may face long-term stagflation in some form.

quotes.text: The reason I say it feels a bit precarious is that today the whole world has a bit of a problem with liquidity peaking.
In the capital market, whoever spends aggressively is seen as impressive, and then when half-year reports are published, it becomes whoever is aggressive gets punished.
Perhaps Nvidia has also reached a point where, in some sense, it needs to use lease-to-buy to drive revenue growth and meet capital market expectations.
Everyone looks and says, if you can pull off this story like that, then I can certainly pull off this story like that too—psychologically it's roughly like that.
The so-called slow bull we always talk about is not because it is inherently both slow and bullish; on the basis of a slow bull, it first needs to create a chip structure.
When the bubble piled up last time had not yet dissipated, a bigger one was added—and added without hesitation.
